title: Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na

questions.prompt: This code stops with `object 'distance' not found`. Why?
questions.code:
flights_new <- flights |>
  filter(month == 10)
  mutate(avg_speed = distance / air_time * 60) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_speed))
choices: The `filter()` line has no `|>` at the end, so `mutate()` runs on its own
questions.explain: Without the pipe, the chain stops after `filter()`. `mutate()` then runs with no data frame, so it can't find `distance`. The error names the symptom, not the cause.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the three rules of tidy data?
choices: Each value is stored as text
questions.explain: Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a cell.

questions.prompt: How many rows does this return?
questions.explain: Without `group_by()`, `summarize()` collapses the whole data frame into a single row.

questions.prompt: Without `na.rm = TRUE`, `mean(dep_delay)` returns `NA` for the `flights` data.
questions.explain: Cancelled flights have no departure delay, and any calculation with an unknown value gives an unknown answer.

questions.prompt: Complete the code so `mean()` skips the missing values.
questions.explain: `na.rm = TRUE` means "remove NAs" before calculating.

questions.prompt: In `summarize(delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))`, what is `delay`?
choices: The name of the new column in the result
questions.explain: You choose the name on the left of `=`; the calculation goes on the right.

questions.prompt: Which function counts the rows in each group, and takes no arguments?
questions.explain: `n()` only works inside dplyr verbs such as `summarize()`. After `group_by()`, it counts the rows in each group.

questions.prompt: Which function returns the middle value?
questions.explain: Half the values are above the median and half below.

questions.prompt: Which function measures how spread out the values are, in the same units as the values?
questions.explain: `sd()` is the standard deviation. `var()`, the variance, is the standard deviation squared, so its units are squared.

questions.prompt: What does `quantile(dep_delay, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)` return?
choices: The delay below which a quarter of the delays fall
A quarter of the mean delay
questions.explain: It is the 25th percentile. For 2013 it is −5 minutes.

questions.prompt: The mean departure delay in 2013 was 12.6 minutes, but the median was −2 minutes. Why?
choices: A few very long delays pull the mean up, but not the median
One of them was calculated wrongly
questions.explain: Delays are skewed: most flights leave close to on time, but a few leave hours late. The median only looks at the middle flight.

questions.prompt: How do you calculate several statistics in one `summarize()`?
choices: Put them in a vector with `c()`
questions.explain: Each pair becomes its own column, still in a single row.

questions.prompt: How many rows does this return?
questions.code:
flights |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(max_delay = max(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
questions.explain: `group_by(month)` makes 12 groups, and `summarize()` returns one row for each.

questions.prompt: How many rows does this return?
questions.explain: There are three origin airports, so three groups and three rows.

questions.prompt: `flights |> group_by(month)` on its own returns 12 rows.
questions.explain: `group_by()` doesn't change the rows. It only notes which group each row is in (`Groups: month [12]`). It takes `summarize()` to collapse each group into one row.

questions.prompt: After `group_by(month) |> summarize(...)`, which column is always in the result?
questions.explain: The grouping column stays, so you can tell the rows apart.

questions.prompt: Complete the code to remove the grouping when you have finished working by group.
questions.code:
flights |>
  group_by(month) |>
  mutate(month_mean = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ___()
questions.explain: `ungroup()` removes the grouping so later steps don't run by group by accident.

questions.prompt: On a data frame grouped by `month`, what does `mutate(m = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))` put in each row?
choices: The mean delay for that flight's month
The mean delay for the whole year
questions.explain: Verbs after `group_by()` work within each group, so the mean is for each month.

questions.prompt: Which package does `drop_na()` come from?
questions.explain: `drop_na()` is in tidyr, which `library(tidyverse)` also loads.

questions.prompt: `drop_na()` with no columns named removes the rows that have an `NA` in:
questions.explain: That can remove more rows than you meant to. Always name the columns your question needs.

questions.prompt: How do `na.rm = TRUE` and `drop_na(dep_delay)` differ?
choices: `drop_na()` removes whole rows for every later step; `na.rm` only affects one calculation
questions.explain: `drop_na()` changes the data. `na.rm = TRUE` only tells one function to skip NAs. Counts with `n()` can differ.

questions.prompt: Why is the mean of the flights' speeds a poor measure of the average speed in a month?
choices: It gives a half-hour hop as much weight as a six-hour flight
Speeds can't be averaged at all
questions.explain: Short flights are slow and plentiful, so they drag the simple mean down. Dividing total distance by total air time counts each flight in proportion to its air time.

questions.prompt: To find the average speed for a month, it is better to divide the total distance by the total air time than to take the mean of the flights' speeds.
questions.explain: That is a weighted average. In January it gives 394 mph, against 370 from the simple mean.

questions.prompt: Put the tiles in order to calculate the weighted speed for each month.
questions.explain: Group, drop the flights with no air time, add up the totals for each month, and then divide the totals.

questions.prompt: Put the tiles in order to find the plane that left late most often.
questions.explain: Keep the late flights, group them by plane, count each group, and sort, largest first.

questions.prompt: `delays` holds six departure delays, one of them missing. Store their mean, skipping the missing value, in `avg_delay`.
questions.solution:
delays <- c(4, -2, NA, 30, 0, -7)
avg_delay <- mean(delays, na.rm = TRUE)
questions.explain: Without `na.rm = TRUE` the answer would be `NA`. The five known delays add up to 25, so the mean is 5.

questions.prompt: `distance` (miles) and `air_time` (minutes) are for three flights. Store their **weighted** average speed in miles per hour, total distance divided by total air time, in `speed`.
questions.solution:
distance <- c(96, 762, 2586)
air_time <- c(32, 116, 345)
speed <- sum(distance) / sum(air_time) * 60
questions.explain: Sum first, then divide: 3,444 miles in 493 minutes is about 419 mph. The mean of the three flights' speeds, `mean(distance / air_time * 60)`, is lower, about 341 mph, because the short flight counts as much as the long one.

questions.prompt: `delays` holds departure delays. Store the number of flights that left late (delay greater than 0) in `n_late`, ignoring the missing value.
questions.solution:
delays <- c(12, -3, NA, 45, 0, 7, -1)
n_late <- sum(delays > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
questions.explain: `delays > 0` is TRUE for 12, 45, and 7. `sum()` counts the TRUEs, as R treats TRUE as 1, and `na.rm = TRUE` skips the NA.
